newsitem.title: UK: Who's afraid of EMU delay? Not the French markets. [CORRECTED 16:03 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Who's afraid of EMU delay? Not the French markets. [CORRECTED 16:03 GMT]

text.p: Not many traders in the franc and French bonds and stocks seem willing to bet that the January 1, 1999 start date for European economic and monetary union (EMU) will be postponed, despite market talk of such a delay.
(Corrects to show the international nature of the market)
France's financial markets have barely flinched during a rumour-strewn couple of weeks, financial analysts said on Tuesday.

Currencies of countries on the European periphery, like the Italian lira, Spanish peseta and Swedish crown, have come under growing pressure in recent weeks as investors reassess their prospects of starting monetary union on time in 1999.
But the extent to which this concern has suddenly mushroomed into fears of a delay to the whole EMU project is still unclear.

Judging by the lack of reaction in French markets to this recent wave of EMU scepticism, either people are not willing to bet against a generalised EMU delay or they think French bond and currency prices would not react to a postponement.
Few believe the latter.

"I think you have to look at the mark/Paris exchange rate and the stability we've seen there is a clear indication that we do not yet have an EMU crisis on our hands," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
"Talk about eventual delay is understandable but the timing is all wrong. Politicians have neither the need nor desire to deal with the delay option for at least another year."
Delay talk is fuelled by concern that record unemployment could mean Germany itself may miss a narrow reading of the budget deficit targets necessary for EMU.

Yet, the letter of the Maastricht Treaty allows for cyclical downturns as well as the budget deficits being "close" to three percent of gross domestic product. How this is read unlikely to be decided until the first candidates for EMU are chosen early next year, analysts said.
None of the current speculation and rumour seems confident enough yet to disturb the core of the EMU bloc.

The German mark/French franc exchange rate is seen by most observers as the lynchpin of monetary union and remains unfazed in the middle of a three-month-old range of just 1.5 centimes around 3.38 francs per mark. That is a band of just 0.4 percent.
Options market pricing shows that one-year implied volatility for this rate, a measure of market expectations of volatility over the next year, is just 2.3 percent.
The bond markets too are similarly unperturbed by talk of EMU delay and French 10-year bond yield spreads are actually trading some 10 basis points below German equivalents.
A favoured analysis of EMU expectations, meantime, is bond yield spreads in the swaps market and these continue to show virtual certainty France will start EMU with Germany in 1999.
Analysts said that if a general EMU delay was seriously being taken on board at the moment arbitrageurs would lock in these price anomalies if they were confident of them shifting. The

most likely explanation is that the latest market movements, which have almost exclusively been isolated to the lira, peseta and crown, have been an acceleration of a paring of over-optimistic convergence trades from last year. Crucially

this has taken place in an environment in which there is concern about a global liquidity squeeze from either a U.S. or Japanese interest rate rise. It has also been stoked by a seasonal repatriation of Japanese funds ahead their fiscal year-end on March 31.
This is partly because much of last year's high-yield convergence plays were funded by cheap yen borrowings.
"The EMU concern is focused on the likes of Italy and Spain and this is primarily a bout of profit taking after a very steep run," said Lee Ferridge, strategist at Commerzbank.
Moreover, most in the market realise that the drive to EMU will be dictated by political will, not least because the wording of the Maastricht Treaty's criteria are so vague.
A chorus of official comments on Monday re-confirming the existing timetable was impressive. "All rumours referring to
EMU delay are not in line with reality," Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer told reporters. "I consider a discussion about the timetable wrong."
"For now at least, Tietmeyer's word is seen as gospel and very few people are really going to run in the face of that," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS. REUTER
